slides.say: If Ron gives Miri four stamps, Miri will have two times as many stamps as Ron will have. Right now, the two of them have the same number of stamps. How many stamps does Miri have now?
at: If Ron gives Miri four stamps

slides.say: We could work the math way. Build an equation, give Ron a letter, move stamps to Miri, and so on. But let's do what we did in this whole lesson, and plug in the answers. The choices are numbers, and the story gives conditions we can check.
Which choice first? None of them is rounder or more convenient than the others. They're all small, easy numbers. So I'll simply start with the first choice, twelve.
They ask how many stamps Miri has now. So let's say Miri has twelve stamps now. How many does Ron have? The story says that right now they have the same number, so Ron also has twelve.
Now Ron gives Miri four stamps. Miri gets four more, twelve plus four, sixteen. Ron has four fewer, twelve minus four, eight.
Is Miri's number twice Ron's? Two times eight is sixteen. Yes. So twelve fits every given, and it's the answer. Choice number one is our answer.
at: Choice number one is our answer

slides: Look at that. This question comes toward the end of the section, so it's supposed to be a very hard one. And once we plugged in the answers, it was really simple.

slides.say: Let's sum up plugging in the answers. When the choices are numbers, and the question gives conditions we can check, we can put each choice into the question and check it.

First we cross out choices that make no sense. Then we start with a round, convenient choice. And when a bigger trial number gives a bigger result, a middle choice can help us rule out more of the ordered choices.

The moment a choice fits every given, we mark it, and we don't need to check the rest. And if three choices are out, the fourth is right, even without checking. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
